name: Google
summary: Practice invariant-driven arrays, graph search, and binary-search prompts aligned with Google-style interviews.

questions.title: Subarray Sum Equals K
questions.summary: Count contiguous subarrays whose sum equals a target value.
questions.prompt: Given an array of integers and a target k, return the number of contiguous subarrays whose values sum to k.

examples.explanation: The first two and last two values both sum to 2.

constraints: Values may be negative, so sliding window is not sufficient.

solutionTracks.title: Prefix Sum Counts
solutionTracks.summary: Count previous prefix sums so each current prefix can identify how many earlier starts produce the target sum.

steps.title: Maintain running sum
steps.explanation: The sum of a subarray ending at the current index is current prefix minus an earlier prefix.

steps.title: Look for prefix minus k
steps.explanation: If current minus target has appeared before, each occurrence starts a valid subarray.

steps.title: Record current prefix
steps.explanation: After counting matches, add the current prefix to support future endings.

solutionTracks.explanation: For any end index, subarray sum equals prefix[end] minus prefix[start before]. Rearranging gives the exact earlier prefix value needed for target k.

solutionTracks.title: Prefix Array Pair Check
solutionTracks.summary: Build prefix sums first, then compare every start and end pair to make the target relationship explicit.

steps.title: Build prefix array
steps.explanation: prefix[i] stores the sum of every item before index i.

steps.title: Try all ranges
steps.explanation: For every start and end, compute prefix[end] minus prefix[start].

steps.title: Count target ranges
steps.explanation: Increment the answer whenever that range sum equals k.

solutionTracks.explanation: This version is slower but useful for deriving the optimized formula. Prefix sums make each candidate range sum O(1) instead of rescanning the range.

questions.title: Word Ladder
questions.summary: Find the shortest one-letter-at-a-time transformation from one word to another.
questions.prompt: Given a begin word, an end word, and a dictionary, return the length of the shortest transformation sequence where each step changes one letter and remains in the dictionary.

examples.explanation: hit, hot, dot, dog, cog has five words.

solutionTracks.title: Breadth-First Word Search
solutionTracks.summary: Treat words as graph nodes and use BFS because every one-letter transformation has equal cost.

steps.title: Queue the start word
steps.explanation: BFS starts with the begin word at distance one and a set of unused dictionary words.

steps.title: Generate neighbors
steps.explanation: For each position, try replacing it with every letter and keep candidates that are in the dictionary.

steps.title: Stop at target
steps.explanation: The first time BFS reaches the end word is the shortest transformation length.

solutionTracks.explanation: BFS explores all paths of length d before any path of length d plus one. Because every transformation costs one, the first end-word discovery is optimal.

solutionTracks.title: Bidirectional BFS
solutionTracks.summary: Search from both begin and end words, always expanding the smaller frontier to reduce the branching work.

steps.title: Keep two frontiers
steps.explanation: One set grows from the begin word and one grows backward from the end word.

steps.title: Expand the smaller side
steps.explanation: Choosing the smaller frontier limits the number of generated one-letter variants.

steps.title: Meet in the middle
steps.explanation: When a generated word exists in the opposite frontier, the two half paths connect.

solutionTracks.explanation: Both searches still use BFS levels, so meeting frontiers gives the shortest path. Expanding the smaller frontier often cuts the explored graph dramatically.

questions.title: Median Of Two Sorted Arrays
questions.summary: Find the median of two sorted arrays without fully sorting their union.
questions.prompt: Given two individually sorted arrays, return the median value across all numbers in both arrays.
constraints: The optimized solution should run in logarithmic time in the shorter array.

solutionTracks.title: Binary Partition
solutionTracks.summary: Binary search the shorter array for a partition where every left-side value is less than every right-side value.

steps.title: Search shorter array
steps.explanation: Using the shorter array bounds the binary search and makes edge cases easier to control.

steps.title: Balance left size
steps.explanation: Choose the matching partition in the second array so the combined left half has the desired size.

steps.title: Validate boundaries
steps.explanation: When left maximums are not greater than right minimums, the partition gives the median immediately.

solutionTracks.explanation: The correct median partition is the place where the combined left half contains the smaller values and the combined right half contains the larger values. Binary search moves toward that boundary.

solutionTracks.title: Partial Merge
solutionTracks.summary: Merge only until the middle positions are known instead of building the full combined array.

steps.title: Walk both arrays
steps.explanation: Use two pointers just like merge sort to consume the smaller next value.

steps.title: Remember two middle values
steps.explanation: Track the previous and current consumed values until the median index is reached.

steps.title: Handle odd and even totals
steps.explanation: Odd totals return the current middle; even totals average previous and current.

solutionTracks.explanation: The merged order defines the median. Stopping after the middle avoids extra work while preserving the exact sequence needed to compute the answer.

questions.title: Number Of Islands
questions.summary: Count connected groups of land in a rectangular grid and compare breadth-first with depth-first flood fill.
questions.prompt: Given a rectangular grid containing 1 for land and 0 for water, return the number of orthogonally connected islands. Solve it once with breadth-first search and once with depth-first search, then explain the practical tradeoffs.

examples.explanation: The upper-left land cells form one island and the lower-right land cells form another.

constraints: Only horizontal and vertical neighbors are connected.
The input grid has at least one row and one column.

diagrams.title: Two connected components
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Top-left land] --- B[Top-left neighbor]
  C[Bottom-right land] --- D[Right neighbor]
  A ~~~ C

solutionTracks.title: BFS Flood Fill
solutionTracks.summary: Scan for unvisited land, count a new island, then use a queue to mark that entire connected component.

steps.title: Scan every cell
steps.explanation: An unvisited land cell begins a connected component that has not been counted yet.

steps.title: Queue the component
steps.explanation: Mark the starting cell visited and process orthogonal land neighbors in FIFO order.

steps.title: Count each start once
steps.explanation: The outer scan increments only when it finds land that no previous flood fill reached.

solutionTracks.explanation: BFS marks every land cell in one connected component before the scan can count it again. It avoids recursion depth risk, though its queue can grow with a wide island frontier.

solutionTracks.title: DFS Flood Fill
solutionTracks.summary: Scan for unvisited land, count a new island, then recursively consume that entire connected component.

steps.title: Define the boundary
steps.explanation: Return when a cell is outside the grid, water, or already visited.

steps.title: Explore one branch
steps.explanation: Mark land and recursively visit its four orthogonal neighbors before returning.

steps.title: Count component roots
steps.explanation: Each outer-scan land cell still unseen is the root of one newly counted island.

solutionTracks.explanation: Recursive DFS closely matches the definition of a connected component and is shorter to read. It has the same asymptotic cost as BFS, but one enormous island can overflow the runtime call stack.

questions.title: Shortest Path In A Binary Matrix
questions.summary: Find the minimum number of equal-cost moves through open cells in a square matrix.
questions.prompt: Given a square binary grid, return the length of the shortest clear path from the top-left cell to the bottom-right cell using eight-direction movement, or -1 when no path exists.

examples.explanation: A diagonal move reaches the destination in a path containing two cells.

constraints: Zero cells are open and one cells are blocked.
Every legal move has equal cost.

solutionTracks.title: Layered BFS
solutionTracks.summary: Explore all grid positions at one path length before advancing to the next length.

steps.title: Reject blocked endpoints
steps.explanation: No route can exist when either the start or destination cell is blocked.

steps.title: Expand one distance layer
steps.explanation: Queue each unseen open neighbor with a distance one greater than its parent.

steps.title: Return first destination
steps.explanation: BFS guarantees that the first destination removed from the queue has minimum distance.

solutionTracks.explanation: The grid is an unweighted graph because every move costs one. BFS processes paths in nondecreasing length, so it can return as soon as the destination is reached.

solutionTracks.title: In-Place Layer BFS
solutionTracks.summary: Reuse the mutable grid as visited state and count one complete queue layer for each path length.

steps.title: Mark the start
steps.explanation: Change the starting open cell to blocked so it cannot be enqueued again.

steps.title: Process one layer
steps.explanation: Every cell currently in the queue has the same shortest path length from the start.

steps.title: Advance the distance
steps.explanation: After one queue layer finishes, increment the path length before expanding the next layer.

solutionTracks.explanation: This BFS keeps the same shortest-path invariant but stores visited state in the grid. It uses less auxiliary bookkeeping, though mutating caller-owned input must be allowed and stated clearly.

questions.title: Course Schedule
questions.summary: Decide whether every course can be completed by detecting a cycle in the prerequisite graph.
questions.prompt: Given a course count and prerequisite pairs, return whether all courses can be completed. Compare depth-first cycle coloring with breadth-first topological processing.

examples.explanation: Each course requires the other, so neither dependency chain can finish.

constraints: Courses are numbered from zero through course count minus one.
Duplicate prerequisite pairs may be ignored.

solutionTracks.title: DFS Three-Color Cycle Detection
solutionTracks.summary: Color each course unseen, visiting, or complete and reject any edge back to the active DFS path.

steps.title: Enter as visiting
steps.explanation: Mark a course as active before recursively checking every dependent course.

steps.title: Detect a back edge
steps.explanation: An edge to another visiting course closes a directed cycle on the current path.

steps.title: Finish as complete
steps.explanation: After every dependency returns safely, mark the course complete so later searches can reuse the result.

solutionTracks.explanation: A directed cycle exists exactly when DFS reaches a node already on its active path. Complete nodes have already been proven safe and need no repeated exploration.

solutionTracks.title: BFS Kahn Topological Processing
solutionTracks.summary: Queue every course with zero prerequisites and remove completed prerequisite edges until no ready course remains.

steps.title: Count incoming edges
steps.explanation: Indegree records how many unmet prerequisites prevent each course from becoming ready.

steps.title: Queue ready courses
steps.explanation: Every zero-indegree course can be completed immediately and processed in BFS order.

steps.title: Compare processed total
steps.explanation: If all courses are removed, the graph is acyclic; a cycle leaves some indegrees positive.

solutionTracks.explanation: Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes nodes that have no remaining prerequisites. A directed cycle has no removable starting point inside the cycle, so the final processed count exposes it.
